paper.one_line_finding: Random assignment to GPT-4o inline suggestions raised the mean cosine similarity between Indian and American essays from 0.48 (SD 0.11) to 0.54 (SD 0.13), t(6958) = −17.89, p < 0.001, d = −0.44 over essay pairs (pp. 9-10, Section 4.3.1), and lowered a classifier's accuracy at telling Indian from American essays from 90.6% to 83.5%, t(38) = 2.25, p = 0.03, d = 0.71 (p. 10, Section 4.3.2).

estimates.measure_detail: Mean cosine similarity of OpenAI text embeddings for every Indian-American essay pair on the same topic, pooled over all writing tasks within each AI condition. The specific embedding model is not named. Higher similarity means less diversity across people.

estimates.control_arm: Indians without AI and Americans without AI (combined)

sources.quote: Overall, 118 participants completed four tasks each, resulting in a dataset of 472 essays. Among these participants, 65 received AI- generated suggestions to aid their writing—36 in India and 29 in the US.
It shows that without AI, the mean similarity between Indians and Americans was 0.48 (𝑆𝐷= 0.11), but with AI, the similarity score rose to 0.54 (𝑆𝐷= 0.13).
revealed that this increase was statistically significant, 𝑡(6958) = −17.89, 𝑝< 0.001.
Further, the effect size of this increase (Cohen’s 𝑑= −0.44)
yielding a distribution of 4 essay topics × (24 × 29) comparisons per topic = 2784 cross-culture similarity scores.

estimates.notes: This is the main full-sample cross-culture similarity contrast. It includes all participants but only cross-country pairs, not all possible pairs within each AI condition. The printed t statistic and Cohen’s d are negative although the AI mean is higher; their direction corresponds to No AI minus AI. Their signs are retained exactly as printed. The paper does not define the standardizer for d. SDs and the t test are over essay pairs, with repeated contributions from each participant and no participant-level clustering reported. Figure 6(b) plots confidence intervals of the arm means, but the endpoints are not printed and are not read from the figure. The combined pair count is not printed, so n_units is null; no count is derived from the degrees of freedom. The pooled No AI participant count is also not printed. The printed No AI pair count is 2784; the AI pair count is not printed. This arm-specific pair count is not a count of people or the combined n_units.

estimates.outcome: Classifier accuracy distinguishing Indian from American authorship, all tasks (%)
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Logistic regression predicts Indian versus American authorship using OpenAI essay embeddings as features, fitted separately for the AI and No AI conditions. The specific embedding model is not named. The mean score is reported in percent; its observations are held-out cross-validation fold scores. Higher classification performance indicates greater distinguishability between cultures, used here as an automated measure of diversity.

stats.difference_is: Decrease from No AI to AI, in percentage points: control minus treatment, as printed.

sources.quote: Overall, 118 participants completed four tasks each, resulting in a dataset of 472 essays. Among these participants, 65 received AI- generated suggestions to aid their writing—36 in India and 29 in the US.
On average, the accuracy decreased by 7.1 percentage points, from 90.6% in the No AI condition to 83.5% in the AI condition.
This decrease was statistically significant, 𝑡(38) = 2.25, 𝑝= 0.03, with a medium effect size (Cohen’s 𝑑= 0.71).
This resulted in a distribution of 20 accuracy and F1 scores in each condition, which we compared using an independent samples t-test.

estimates.notes: This is an output-based cultural-distinguishability measure, not a convergent test taken by participants. The classifier is a scoring method; it is not an AI-treatment regression, so regression is null. The independent-samples t test treats cross-validation fold scores as observations; unit and se_basis are set. No participant-level or participant-clustered uncertainty, fold-score SDs, SEs, or confidence intervals are printed. The printed t statistic and Cohen’s d follow No AI minus AI and are retained without reversing their signs; the standardizer is not defined. The total number of fold-score observations is not printed and is not computed by adding the per-condition counts. The pooled No AI participant count is not printed. Means remain in percent, with no conversion to proportions.

open_items: The paper prints analyzed participant counts but no counts at random assignment, noncompletion, or post-assignment exclusion under the lifelong-country-residence rule. Both task completion and the demographic survey were required after assignment at consent (PDF pp. 4-5).

The combined No AI participant count is not printed. n_control remains null; the country-specific control counts are preserved in the study arms. For all retained full-sample analyses, n_treatment and n_total use the printed completed-study counts (PDF p. 3, Table 1; PDF p. 7, Section 4).

The paper provides no participant-level SD or participant-level/participant-clustered uncertainty for similarity or classifier outcomes. Similarity uncertainty is over essay pairs; classifier uncertainty is over model-performance scores on sets of essays. These are not participant-level standard errors (PDF pp. 9-11). No data or code repository is identified.

The AI and combined cross-culture pair counts and the combined all-task classifier fold-score count are not printed. The email-specific fold count is not stated. No counts are inferred from degrees of freedom or calculated by adding per-condition counts (PDF pp. 9-11).

Numerical confidence-interval endpoints for cross-culture similarity appear only graphically. Classifier arm SDs, SEs, and confidence intervals are not printed. The standardizer for each reported Cohen’s d is undefined (PDF pp. 9-11).

Embedding-dimension sensitivity results are plotted without numerical contrasts, and essay length is described only narratively. Their full-sample records retain null statistics. The essay-length n_units is the printed complete essay corpus, not a separately reported length-test sample size (PDF p. 6, Section 3.5.2; PDF p. 7, Section 4; PDF p. 11, Section 4.3.3; PDF p. 12, Figure 8).
The exact OpenAI embedding model, GPT-4o release year, and dated GPT-4o API snapshot are not stated. ai_tool.year remains null (PDF pp. 4-5, Section 3.3.2; PDF p. 7, Section 3.5.2).
The citation record identifies a later ACM publication version. This reconciliation verifies the saved arXiv v3 only; differences from the ACM version of record remain unverified.

The Indian public-figure aggregate in the prose is flagged as inconsistent with Appendix B by the screening form. This country-subgroup outcome is excluded under rule 5; no replacement aggregate or share is computed here (PDF p. 13, Section 4.4.3; PDF p. 20, Table 7).

The full-sample similarity measure uses cross-country pairs only, rather than every possible pair within each AI condition. No pooled within-country AI contrast is printed. The choice of primary across_people record remains a synthesis decision; no preregistered primary outcome is stated (PDF pp. 9-11).

review_corrections.basis: The task (short personal texts and an email) qualifies through across-writer similarity; its quality, readability, and length scores measure writing, not creativity (Review 1 Decisions 7 and 10; codebook section 1, sentence added 2026-10-11 for review). Construct other: shown on the study page, never primary or pooled.
